title: Strong Password Checker II
constraints: password contains only letters, digits and the special characters !@#$%^&*()-+
notes:
## Intuition

Every rule can be checked while reading the password once. Four flags remember which kinds of character have appeared, and comparing each character with the one before it catches a repeated neighbour the moment it happens. Only the length needs no scan at all.

## Approach

1. If `password` is shorter than 8 characters, return `false` straight away.
2. Set `hasLower`, `hasUpper`, `hasDigit` and `hasSpecial` to `false`.
3. For each index `i`, read `ch`. If it equals the previous character, return `false`.
4. Otherwise classify `ch` by its range (`a`–`z`, `A`–`Z`, `0`–`9`) or by membership in `special`, and set that flag.
5. After the loop the password is strong exactly when all four flags are `true`.

## Example 1, step by step

`password = "IloveLe3tcode!"` has 14 characters, so the length check passes. `I` sets `hasUpper`, `l` sets `hasLower`, `3` sets `hasDigit` and the final `!` sets `hasSpecial`. No character equals the one before it (`Le`, `e3`, `de`... all differ), so the loop finishes and all four flags are `true`: the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over the characters.
- Space: O(1): four flags and the fixed `special` string.

## Pitfalls

- The repeat rule is about neighbours only: `"aba"` is allowed, `"aab"` is not.
- In a regular expression, `-` inside `[...]` makes a range unless escaped or placed last; comparing against a plain string avoids that trap.
- Checking only the flags and forgetting the length (or the other way round) passes many tests but fails short strong-looking passwords.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `special` | the twelve allowed special characters |
| `hasLower`, `hasUpper`, `hasDigit`, `hasSpecial` | whether each required kind has been seen |
| `i` | index of the current character |
| `ch` | the current character |
